claims.text: Selective oxidation of the reactive alloying element governs protective-oxide formation and stability in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Increasing Al or Si content promotes a coherent, slow-growing Al2O3- or SiO2-rich oxide layer.
Al2O3- or SiO2-rich scales adhere well because they minimize lattice and thermal stresses.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNi alloys tend to form mixed Mn-oxide scales that are less coherent than Al- or Si-rich scales.
Mixed Mn-oxide scales crack or spall above 900 °C.
Oxidative exposure near 950 °C produces an oxide scale on the Al-containing CrFeCoNi alloy system.
A dense Al2O3 or SiO2 sublayer has low lattice mismatch with the underlying alloy.
Reduced oxide–alloy lattice mismatch reduces interfacial stress accumulation.
Al and Si preferentially oxidize relative to the other constituent elements.
A continuous, adherent Al2O3- or SiO2-rich layer acts as a diffusion barrier and thereby slows further oxidation.
Mn oxides cannot accommodate thermal and mechanical stresses, causing cracking and spallation.
Under identical exposure conditions, Al- or Si-enriched alloys will exhibit slower oxide growth and less spallation than Mn-containing alloys.
Comparable alloys with lower Al or Si levels, or without Al or Si, form less coherent and more failure-prone oxide layers.
High-temperature oxidation of an AlCoCrFeNi material can involve elemental redistribution and matrix phase transformation.
